title: Early Quran Manuscripts: What the Physical Evidence Shows
subtitle: The Birmingham fragment, the Sanaa palimpsest, and the Samarkand and Topkapi codices, and what they do and do not prove
summary: Early Quran manuscripts strongly support a text close to the one read today. Early fragments, recitation, and the Uthmanic standard work together in the preservation case. Radiocarbon dates parchment, not ink, and no fragment proves every verse by itself.

seo.metaTitle: Early Quran Manuscripts: Birmingham, Sanaa, Samarkand Explained
seo.metaDescription: Early Quran manuscripts provide physical evidence for a text very close to the one read today.

sections.title: The Evidence in Brief
sections.body: Early Quran manuscripts give physical evidence for a text close to today's. Birmingham, Parisino-petropolitanus, and other witnesses preserve parts of the Uthmanic consonantal text. Radiocarbon dates parchment, not ink. The evidence is cumulative: no single leaf tells the whole story.

sections.title: What Manuscripts Can Establish
sections.body: A manuscript can show that wording existed early. Script study and radiocarbon help estimate its age. Each method has limits. Radiocarbon dates parchment, not writing, so its range is an estimate rather than an exact writing date.

sections.title: The Quran's Own Claim: A Preserved Tablet
sections.body:
The Quran makes a theological claim about preservation. Surah Al-Buruj says: "But this is an honored Qur'an, [Inscribed] in a Preserved Slate" (Quran 85:21–22). Muslims understand this as a heavenly original. A laboratory cannot settle a faith claim.

The [University of Birmingham reports](https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/facilities/cadbury/birmingham-quran-mingana-collection/birmingham-quran/what-is) that Oxford dated the parchment to AD 568–645 at 95.4 percent confidence. Its leaves contain parts of Surahs 18–20. The date applies to parchment, not ink. This supports early writing alongside memorization.

sections.title: For Comparison: The Bible's Earliest Complete Manuscripts
sections.body:
Christian scripture does not make the same heavenly-tablet claim. Christian scholars compare manuscripts to seek early wording. This is a method, not a criticism of Christian scholarship.

[Codex Sinaiticus](https://codexsinaiticus.org/en/codex/) dates to the fourth century and preserves the earliest complete surviving New Testament. Vaticanus is another major fourth-century biblical codex, though parts are missing. Both are earlier in calendar time than the seventh-century Birmingham Quran leaves. The meaningful comparison is the interval from each text's origin to its surviving copies. Early fragments must be compared with fragments, and larger codices with larger codices. This prevents an unfair comparison while allowing the Quran's early manuscript evidence to be assessed on its own merits.

sections.title: A Dual Transmission System
sections.body: The Quran was transmitted by memorization and writing in the first community. Manuscripts confirm a text carried by reciters. The New Testament survived through decentralized copies with variants. Both traditions have evidence, but the Quran had early oral and written coordination.

sections.title: Common Questions About Early Copies
sections.body: No fragment contains the whole Quran. Radiocarbon is not an exact writing date. Spelling differences do not automatically create a different text. The question is early stability, and the answer is broad support. Early witnesses support the consonantal skeleton and recited content while allowing study of spelling and readings.

sections.title: Why the Manuscripts Matter
sections.body: Quran 15:9 promises preservation. Islam teaches that God preserved the Quran. Muslims believe the early witnesses fit that promise. Manuscripts also fit the history of public recitation, early writing, standardization, and memorization. The promise is theological; the manuscript evidence is physical.

sections.title: The Central Takeaway
sections.body: Early manuscripts give unusually early evidence for the text recited today. Alongside memorization, compilation reports, and readings, they give historical reason to take preservation seriously. Faith remains necessary, but evidence can help.

- **Qur'ans of the Umayyads** — François Déroche.
- **Textual Criticism and Qur'an Manuscripts** — Keith E. Small.
- **Misquoting Jesus** — Bart D. Ehrman.

faq.question: Is the Birmingham Quran fragment really the oldest Quran manuscript in the world?
faq.answer: It is one of the oldest known Quran fragments. Oxford dated its parchment to AD 568–645 with 95.4 percent confidence. A few other early fragments have overlapping date ranges, so no single fragment can be called the oldest with certainty.

faq.question: Does the Sanaa palimpsest mean the Quran we have today is wrong?
faq.answer: No. Its lower text has real differences from the standard Uthmanic rasm. Scholars debate how that early layer relates to standardization. The upper text follows the Uthmanic tradition, and the wider record shows that this text became dominant early and remained stable.

faq.question: Are the Samarkand and Topkapi codices really Uthman's personal copies?
faq.answer: That is a popular tradition. Specialists who study the script usually date both codices after Uthman's lifetime. Their personal attribution to him is therefore devotional tradition, not a confirmed manuscript fact.

faq.question: How does the Quran's manuscript record compare to the Bible's?
faq.answer: Some Quran fragments date within decades of Muhammad's death. The earliest complete or nearly complete Bible codices are from the fourth century. Earlier New Testament papyri also survive, but they are fragments rather than complete Bibles.

faq.question: Does manuscript evidence prove the Quran is divinely preserved?
faq.answer: No single object can prove a claim about God. Manuscripts show the history of writing and copying. The Quran's promise is a faith claim, while its early and stable witnesses provide strong historical support for it.
